entries.clue: Bugs belonging to groups (7)

blocks.note: to belong to a club is to be in it
a sect is a breakaway religious group

annotation.surface: Creepy-crawlies sorted out by the group each one belongs to.
annotation.walkthrough: Written out, the wordplay reads 'in sects', which says much the same thing as the clue's own words while spelling something else entirely. Only the first word stands outside that phrase, and it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Bugs is the loose everyday word for small crawling and flying creatures, and insects are what people mean by it.

entries.clue: Accepted group member, right, supporting trendy team (7)

indicatorNotes.supporting: Something that supports another thing holds it up from underneath, and in a down entry underneath means later in the answer.

blocks.note: in = trendy, whatever is currently fashionable
a side is a team in British sports talk — Arsenal are a side
r = right

annotation.surface: A club member in good standing who, quite rightly, backs a fashionable team.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' looks like the fan in the surface and is really a position: what holds something up in a down entry ends below it, so the single letter lands last rather than first.
annotation.definitionFit: An insider is a member let inside a group's confidence, somebody the group has accepted rather than merely enrolled.

entries.clue: Males involved in witch-hunt town (5)

indicatorNotes.involved: Something involved is tangled up in something else, and tangled letters do not come out in the order they went in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: The men caught up in the business of a town's witch-hunt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Involved' works twice over: caught up in something on the surface, tangled underneath. Nothing else in the sentence points at New England, which is the only place the answer could be.
annotation.definitionFit: Salem, in Massachusetts, held the 1692 witch trials, and its name has stood for a witch-hunt ever since.

entries.clue: Angry journalist marked with an 'X' (7)

blocks.note: cross is the mild word for angry, the one a parent uses
ed = editor, the journalist at the top of the paper

annotation.surface: A bad-tempered reporter who has put an X against something.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end and reads like a description of the journalist, which is what keeps the break hidden. 'Ed' is the crossword's standard newspaperman and turns up in dozens of puzzles.
annotation.definitionFit: An X is a cross, so anything bearing one has been crossed — the same verb used of crossing a name off a list.

entries.clue: Seconds regularly relent (6)

blocks.note: s = seconds, the unit's abbreviation
something done regularly is done often

annotation.surface: Second helpings handed round often enough that anyone would give in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' is the trap: in a cryptic it almost always asks you to take every other letter, and here it is a plain synonym. Nothing is being skipped over at all.
annotation.definitionFit: To soften and to relent are the same movement — a hard position giving way to a gentler one.

entries.clue: Copying a sharp ringing sound (5)

blocks.note: the article is taken as the single letter it is
the short high note that struck metal or a microwave oven makes

annotation.surface: Someone doing an impression of a bright little chime.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one phrase about mimicry and the break falls after its very first word. To ape somebody is to copy the way an ape is said to copy, so the verb keeps a mocking edge.
annotation.definitionFit: Aping is copying: imitating another's manner closely, and closely enough to send it up.

entries.clue: Kipling's lone wolf under a stormy lake (5)

indicatorNotes.under: What is under something in a down entry sits below it, so those letters follow the ones above.
indicatorNotes.stormy: A storm throws loose things about, and letters thrown about land in a new order.

blocks.note: the article is taken as the single letter it is
the four letters of LAKE re-set

annotation.surface: A solitary wolf sheltering below a lake whipped up by bad weather.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A stormy lake' paints the weather while quietly naming the letters and the shuffle, and 'under' then says which half goes on top. British Cub Scout packs still call their leader by this name.
annotation.definitionFit: Akela is Kipling's great grey Lone Wolf, head of the Seeonee pack in The Jungle Book.

entries.clue: Thankless type breaking granite (7)

indicatorNotes.breaking: Break something and the pieces no longer sit where they did, so the letters are re-set.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Somebody ungrateful smashing up a block of granite.
annotation.walkthrough: Granite is the hardest thing in the clue and the one word the setter asks you to break, which is the joke the surface is built on. 'Type' is the noun for a person here, nothing to do with printing.
annotation.definitionFit: An ingrate gives no thanks for what they have been given — thankless in the older sense, describing the ungrateful one rather than the job.

entries.clue: Scrambled egg to start in New York (3-2)

indicatorNotes.Scrambled: Scrambled eggs are beaten out of any order at all, and scrambled letters go the same way.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A scrambled-egg breakfast ordered as a starter in a New York diner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scrambled egg' hides one of the tidiest anagram signals going, because indicator and fodder sit inside a phrase everybody already says together. The 3-2 enumeration is the tell that a hyphenated idiom is coming.
annotation.definitionFit: From the get-go is American for from the very beginning, so the get-go is the start — a phrase you hear in New York, not London.

entries.clue: Also involved a small number in the gun discharge (5)

indicatorNotes.involved: Something involved is tangled, and tangled letters come out in a different order from the one they went in.
indicatorNotes.in: A thing put in another sits inside it, between its letters rather than alongside them.

blocks.note: the four letters of ALSO re-set, then opened up after the third
v is the Roman five, small as numbers go

annotation.surface: A modest figure caught up in the moment the guns went off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the gun discharge' reads as one phrase and is really two jobs, the insertion and then the definition. Roman numerals are the usual answer when a clue asks vaguely for a small number.
annotation.definitionFit: A salvo is the simultaneous discharge of guns, the volley loosed off by a whole battery at once.

entries.clue: Cargo of crashed fighter (7)

indicatorNotes.crashed: A crash leaves the parts scattered, so the letters come to rest in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: The load recovered from a fighter plane that came down.
annotation.walkthrough: A crashed fighter is a picture rather than a description of letters, and that is the whole of the clue's disguise. Anagrams of a single ordinary word are the ones solvers most often walk straight past.
annotation.definitionFit: Freight is the goods a ship, train or lorry carries, which is what cargo names as well.

entries.clue: Send me off to English estate (7)

indicatorNotes.off: Milk that has gone off has turned, and letters told to turn will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
e = English, joined to the fodder before the shuffle
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Asking to be packed off to a country house somewhere in England.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Send me off' is a complete instruction on the surface and a complete instruction underneath, which is what makes it so easy to read past. The word is said 'di-MEEN', and looks far stranger on the page than it sounds.
annotation.definitionFit: A demesne is the land attached to a manor and kept by its owner rather than let out, an estate in the old legal sense.

entries.clue: In total, a momentous American battle (5)

indicatorNotes.In: What is in something lies inside it, so the letters are already written out within the words that follow.

blocks.note: the last two letters of 'total' run on through 'a' into the first two of 'momentous'

annotation.surface: A battle fought in America that added up to something momentous.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma falls exactly where the buried letters need it to, which is why the sentence sits so flat on the page. 'In' looks like ordinary scene-setting and is the clue's only instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: The Alamo is the San Antonio mission where a Texan garrison was wiped out in 1836, and the place name stands for the battle itself.

entries.clue: Live with front off chair (6)

indicatorNotes.front off: The front of a word is the letter it starts with, and taking that off leaves the rest standing.

blocks.note: to chair a meeting is to preside over it
the front letter of PRESIDE is the P, and off it comes

annotation.surface: Making do at home with a chair whose front has come away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chair' is the verb, not the furniture — what a chairman does to a meeting. Putting 'front off' immediately beside it is what keeps the furniture reading alive for as long as it lasts.
annotation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to live there, the formal verb a form reaches for when it wants your address.

entries.clue: Making his extremely cold (7)

indicatorNotes.Making: Making something is forming it anew out of what you were handed, so the letters are rebuilt in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, three letters
extremely and very are the same intensifier, and its four letters join the fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Chilling something of his right down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an instruction to take a word's outermost letters and is nothing of the kind — it is a plain synonym, and its four letters are more than half the fodder. 'Cold' at the end is the definition, adjective for adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone shivery is cold, in the sense of the shaking chill a person feels rather than the temperature of a thing.

entries.clue: Single man deprived of a grave (6)

indicatorNotes.deprived of: To be deprived of something is to have it taken away from you, so that letter is missing from the word it names.

blocks.note: sole and single both mean the only one
the three letters are written out in the clue
the article names the letter dropped from MAN

annotation.surface: An unmarried man denied even a grave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grave' is the adjective, weighty and serious, not the hole in the ground the surface digs. The deletion is unusually polite about itself, since the letter to be removed is spelt out for you.
annotation.definitionFit: Solemn and grave are the same adjective for a serious, unsmiling manner — a solemn face and a grave face are one face.

entries.clue: Not even the head displays a strange quality (7)

blocks.note: a number is either even or odd, so not even is odd
a ness is a headland, the sense kept alive in place names like Inverness and Sheerness

annotation.surface: Not even the person in charge shows any sign of strangeness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not even' carries the surface's denial and is a definition in its own right, the opposite of an even number. A ness is a headland, and Britain's coastline is dotted with them.
annotation.definitionFit: Oddness is the quality of being odd — the strangeness itself, rather than the strange thing that has it.

entries.clue: Orderly surrounds wild sow - it's a piece of cake! (2,5)

indicatorNotes.surrounds: To surround something is to close round it on every side, so this word splits and the other goes between the halves.
indicatorNotes.wild: Something wild is out of all control, and letters out of control will not keep the order they were given.

blocks.note: an orderly desk is a neat one, and these four letters open up after the first
the three letters of SOW re-set

annotation.surface: A hospital orderly cornering an escaped pig, and finding it easy enough.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Orderly' is the adjective, not the hospital porter the surface offers. The dash marks the point where the wordplay stops and the exclamation that defines it begins.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for something easy: a piece of cake is done without trouble, and no sweat says the same by naming the effort it did not cost.

entries.clue: Elected party given alternative sort of sports (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names a category rather than offering a synonym: the answer is the adjective that marks that category out from the rest.

blocks.note: a candidate who wins a seat is in — election-night language on British television
a do is a party: an office do, a works do
or is the word that offers the alternative in any choice of two

annotation.surface: A newly elected party handed a different kind of sporting fixture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elected party' is one phrase on the surface and two separate pieces underneath, and the political reading holds right up to the final word. All three pieces are ordinary words rather than abbreviations.
annotation.definitionFit: Indoor is the adjective naming a whole class of sport — squash, badminton, five-a-side — played under a roof instead of on a field.

entries.clue: Little one hid round back of school after caught (5)

indicatorNotes.round: Something that goes round another closes on both sides of it, so this word splits to let the letter in.
indicatorNotes.back of: The back of a word is the letter at its end, and only that one is taken.
indicatorNotes.after: Whatever comes after something else is written behind it, so the piece named last in the clue is placed first in the answer.

blocks.note: c = caught, the cricket scorecard's mark for a catch
the three letters are written out in the clue and open up after the second
the back of SCHOOL is its last letter

annotation.surface: A youngster caught out, then hiding round the back of the school.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round back of school' is a real place on the surface and three separate instructions underneath. C for caught comes off a cricket scorecard, where 'c Smith b Jones' records who took the catch.
annotation.definitionFit: A little one is what parents and nurses call a small child — the age is what is meant, not the height.

entries.clue: Share that is for sweet little thing (5)

blocks.note: your cut of the takings is your share of them
i.e. is short for the Latin id est, that is

annotation.surface: A share set aside for somebody small and adorable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Share' is the noun a gangster uses about the proceeds, not the verb the surface offers. 'That is' spells out its abbreviation in full English rather than hinting at it.
annotation.definitionFit: A cutie is an affectionate name for somebody small and pretty, the noun made straight out of 'cute'.

entries.clue: Monotonous talk from first medic? (5)

blocks.note: dr = doctor, and a medic is one
the first in any order is number one

annotation.surface: Dull talk coming from the doctor who got there first.
annotation.walkthrough: Written out, the two pieces read 'Dr One' — which is what a first medic would be, taken absolutely at its word, and the question mark is the setter owning up to it. The definition is a noun, the sound of a voice, not a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A drone is speech running on at one dull unchanging pitch, the noun for the sound a monotonous talker makes.

entries.clue: Those barely there? (7)

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: people who are only just present, hanging on at the edge of a roll-call
the reading the setter means: barely as in bare, so these are the people who are there with nothing on

annotation.surface: People who only just managed to turn up at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Only just present' is the sense the sentence offers and it is the wrong one; the question mark is the standard warning that a clue is a definition at play. Nothing here is taken apart letter by letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Hear 'barely' as bare rather than scarcely and the clue describes exactly the people who go about with no clothes on.

entries.clue: Worker left police officer with material (5)

indicatorNotes.left: Somebody who has left has gone from where they were, so those letters are no longer in the word.

blocks.note: a sergeant is the rank above constable in a British police force
the ant is the crossword's standard worker, and its three letters are the ones that go

annotation.surface: A workman walks out, leaving a police officer holding a bolt of cloth.
annotation.walkthrough: The worker is inside the police officer rather than standing beside him, and 'left' is what takes him out again. 'Ant' for worker is among the first conventions worth learning.
annotation.definitionFit: Serge is a hard-wearing twilled worsted, the cloth school blazers and old suits were cut from — material in the tailor's sense.

entries.clue: Lot more confused by the musical effect (7)

indicatorNotes.confused: Confused things are mixed up and out of their proper places, and so are the letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Still more of the audience baffled by what the band is doing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lot more confused' reads as one complete idea, which is what stops you seeing its first two words as letters. The definition is only the last two words; 'by the' carries no instruction at all.
annotation.definitionFit: Tremolo is the trembling repetition or wavering of a note a player gets by shaking the bow or the string — an effect, not a tune.

entries.clue: Weird, last piece of wreckage found on a great lake (5)

indicatorNotes.last piece of: The last piece of a word is the letter at its end, and that single letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: the final letter of WRECKAGE
Erie is one of the five Great Lakes on the border between the United States and Canada

annotation.surface: A scrap of debris washed up on the shore of one of the Great Lakes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Great lake' is capitalised in an atlas and not in the clue, and that lower case is the whole of the disguise. Once the definition is separated off the front, the two halves sit in the order the clue gives them.
annotation.definitionFit: Eerie is weird in its unsettling sense — strange in a way that raises the hairs, rather than merely unusual.

entries.clue: Emerging first, variety of jaguar (1-4)

indicatorNotes.first: The first of a word is the letter it begins with, and only that letter is wanted.

blocks.note: the opening letter of EMERGING
a variety of something is a type of it

annotation.surface: A big cat coming out ahead of the others, one of the rarer varieties.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Variety of jaguar' is the trap: it reads as one definition and is really two jobs, with only the last word defining. The 1-4 enumeration tells you a single letter comes first.
annotation.definitionFit: The E-Type is Jaguar's 1961 sports car, so naming the marque points at one particular and very famous model of it.

entries.clue: Admire ornate sceptre (7)

indicatorNotes.ornate: Ornate work has been elaborately worked over, and letters worked over come out rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Standing in admiration before a heavily decorated royal staff.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ornate' is exactly the word anybody would reach for about a sceptre, which is why it does not look like an instruction. The definition is the verb, something you do, rather than the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: To respect somebody is to admire them, holding them in regard rather than merely being polite to them.
